newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin returns to Russia woes from Helsinki summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin returns to Russia woes from Helsinki summit.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin returns on Saturday from a Helsinki summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton that was dominated by NATO's expansion plans, to complete his cabinet reshuffle and tackle painful domestic problems.

Yeltsin's communist opponents were quick to denounce the results of the meeting in the Finnish capital as a "crushing defeat" for Moscow, but there has been no reaction yet from other segments of the Russian political spectrum.

Once home, Yeltsin is expected to put the finishing touches to a major government shake-up aimed at speeding up stalled reforms and loosening the stranglehold caused by delayed wage payments and non-payment of debts between enterprises.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, Yeltsin's rival in the presidential election last summer, compared the Helsinki summit with the Versailles Treaty of 1919, which ended World War One and imposed humiliating conditions on Germany, the loser.
"Yeltsin's foreign policy suffered a crushing defeat," Interfax quoted Zyuganov as saying. "In fact the Helsinki agreements are Russia's Versailles."

Yeltsin and Clinton agreed to differ on the eastward expansion of NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation), but said Moscow would still negotiate a partnership agreement with the alliance, which they hoped could be signed before the NATO summit in July.
Yeltsin and his conservative foes were equally critical of NATO's plans to grant membership to Moscow's former Cold War allies.

But in contrast to Yeltsin, who focused on working out a deal that would further at least some of Moscow's aims, Russian hardliners have insisted on uncompromising opposition to NATO expansion, regardless of the results achieved.
Most other political groups here had been much more pragmatic about Russia's ability to stop NATO's eastward enlargement, and about its need for a good deal with the alliance.
Yeltsin's cooperative attitude to Clinton only added to the fury of Russian hardliners already angered by the cabinet reshuffle, in which young aggressive reformers rose to top cabinet positions.

Yeltsin named his chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, 41, a hate-figure for conservatives for his role in Russia's bold privatisation campaign, as first deputy prime minister and appointed other reformers to the government.

"The changes in the government have been prompted by the needs of the current stage of economic reforms," Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told the communist-dominated State Duma lower house on Friday, explaining the cabinet changes.
The deputies are not the only ones who are demanding explanations from the government.
Trade unions are planning nationwide protest action on March 27 to demand urgent steps from the cabinet. Chernomyrdin has sent new government members to regions where the situation is most tense.

Chubais went to the mining region of Kemerovo to take part in a coal miners' union conference on Friday. Miners were among Yeltsin's most loyal backers in the early 1990s but are now disenchanted with reform.
Bearing a message of goodwill from Yeltsin and about $30 million in back wages, Chubais vowed to pay all wage arrears by the end of the year and to clear the pensions backlog by June.
Chernomyrdin is expected to hold a telephone conference with influential regional governors on Saturday to urge them to make extra efforts to clear such backlogs.
